A significant challenge in speech recognition is the scarcity of labeled data, which can be addressed by leveraging the vast amount of unlabeled data available. Semi-supervised learning (SSL) has been a widely used approach to tackle this problem. This study introduces a new SSL method for speech recognition, which incorporates a contrastive loss function to enhance the connections between similar data points and minimize those between dissimilar data points. The proposed approach, dubbed the Contrastive Twin Network (CTN), is evaluated on the LibriSpeech dataset and demonstrates a notable improvement of 0.5% in word error rate over a baseline model trained solely on labeled data.

The framework approach to lepton-nucleon scattering is explored, with emphasis on the axial and vector framework functions in inelastic channels. A 2021 update to previous framework developments is presented, addressing progress made in this area of study.

This study focuses on almost-sure stabilizing adaptive control for linear-quadratic systems influenced by hidden Markov chains. Initially, we establish the existence of such a control mechanism before examining its design through two distinct approaches. Firstly, we explore the scenario where the system is controllable from any state, regardless of its corresponding hidden state. Secondly, we consider cases where the system's controllability is conditional upon the current state, which may vary. In both scenarios, we demonstrate that the control mechanism can be optimized by solving a series of coupled Riccati equations. Furthermore, we present a method to determine the necessary solution to these equations through an iterative process. Finally, we validate our theoretical findings with numerical examples.

A growing interest in neuroscience has been sparked by the active inference theory, which posits that the human brain operates as an inference engine, driven by the minimization of surprise. This principle is rooted in the free energy framework, which has been expanded to include the processing of multiple sensory inputs and factors. This work presents a novel approach to active inference, which incorporates the processing of multiple sensory inputs and factors, and is demonstrated through its application to a simulated multi-agent system. The results show that the proposed model outperforms existing models, which are limited to single-factor and single-sensory input processing, in terms of performance and efficiency. The proposed model is particularly well-suited for the simulation of complex, real-world scenarios, and has the potential to be applied to a wide range of multi-agent systems.

We examine the propagation of small-amplitude ion acoustic waves in a quark-gluon plasma, accounting for the effects of temperature and quantum statistics. Building upon the Korteweg-de Vries equation, we derive a modified version that takes into consideration temperature and quantum statistics. Our analysis reveals that this modified equation yields a soliton solution, which we refer to as a KdV-type soliton. We then investigate the impact of temperature and quantum statistics on the properties of this soliton, including its amplitude, width, and velocity. Our findings indicate that the soliton's characteristics are significantly influenced by temperature and quantum statistics.

We explore the concept of isochronocity in a one-dimensional system of interacting particles, where the dynamics of particles are influenced by their position relative to one another. Our analysis reveals that isochronocity is achievable in this setting, and we derive the conditions necessary for isochronocity to occur. To demonstrate our findings, we employ the technique of normal form theory and provide an explicit, parametric example of isochronocity.

The Lorenz system, a simplified model of fluid convection, is known to produce complex patterns, including chaotic behavior and simple or complex periodic orbits, depending on the Rayleigh number and Prandtl number. These periodic orbits, which are believed to be the underlying structure of chaotic attractors, are difficult to identify due to their transient nature. Researchers have developed a novel method to identify and classify periodic orbits by analyzing the similarity signature of the system's time series. This method has been successfully applied to the Lorenz system, revealing the existence of various periodic orbits, including those that are difficult to detect using traditional methods. The results of this study provide new insights into the structure of the Lorenz system and its ability to produce complex patterns.

Our approach is based on the concept of the relative entropy of a certain class of probability measures, which are defined on a suitable function space.

This study explores the Teichmüller metric on the moduli space of Riemann surfaces with specified punctures and boundary components, as well as its lift to unit tangent bundles. The metric is defined by the infimum of lengths of specific curves, and its behavior is analyzed in relation to a given metric on the surface. The main result establishes a connection between the Teichmüller metric and the spectrum of a deformed Laplacian, and its implications are discussed.

We introduce FNetAR, a novel autoregressive language model that leverages a Fourier neural network (FNet) architecture to process input tokens in a continuous manner. By blending tokens with autoregressive Fourier transforms, FNetAR achieves efficient parallelization and significantly reduces computational overhead. Our results demonstrate that FNetAR outperforms the Transformer in various downstream tasks, including language modeling, text classification, and machine translation, while maintaining comparable model capacity. Notably, FNetAR exhibits enhanced robustness to adversarial attacks and is less susceptible to overfitting.

The process of annotating audio data for machine learning purposes involves a crucial step, which is often hindered by the complexity of existing taxonomies. This complexity can result in confusion and ambiguity, ultimately slowing down the annotation process. To address this issue, we conducted a study to explore the challenges faced by annotators and to identify potential solutions that can streamline the process. Our research involved a combination of a survey and a user study, which revealed that annotators struggle with large taxonomies and that providing a search function and clear descriptions can significantly improve the annotation experience. Our findings suggest that these interventions can lead to a substantial reduction in time spent annotating, thereby making the process more efficient.

The core concept of dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT) is to break down a complex many-body problem into a simpler two-body problem, which can be effectively solved using density matrix renormalization group (DMRG) methods. This approach is particularly useful for studying systems with multiple quantum states, such as reaction networks, where the DMFT method can be applied to analyze the dynamics of quantum systems with multiple possible outcomes. In this paper, we explore the application of DMFT to study quantum reaction networks, and we demonstrate its effectiveness by analyzing a specific example of a system with multiple quantum states, such as the reaction of two identical particles to form a single particle with multiple possible outcomes. We also discuss the implications of this approach for understanding the dynamics of complex quantum systems, and we highlight its potential for future research in this area.

We have investigated the statistical properties of avalanche sizes in a model of an infinite Cayley tree, where a percolation process is simulated. In this model, each bond on the tree has a probability $p$ of being occupied, and an avalanche occurs when a certain number of occupied bonds, starting from a randomly chosen bond, become activated. We have found that the distribution of avalanche sizes follows a power law, with a critical exponent that depends on the probability $p$. Our results are in agreement with previous studies, and we have also derived an exact formula for the avalanche size distribution.

A novel approach to safeguarding quantum information against errors has been discovered through the integration of topological photonics.  Topological photonics offers a way to create robust photonic states that are protected against local disturbances.  In this research, we have developed a method to create and protect a one-dimensional topological state of squeezed light on a chip-scale circuit.  Our scheme utilizes a unique type of squeezed vacuum state that is generated by a nonlinear process, and we have demonstrated that this state can be protected against errors by creating a topological state of light.  Furthermore, we have shown that this scheme can be used to create a protected qubit that is robust against decoherence, and we have provided a detailed analysis of the error rates and their dependence on the system parameters.  Our results have important implications for the development of fault-tolerant quantum computing and quantum communication systems.

This research introduces an innovative method for generating optimal trajectories for drones, which can be seamlessly integrated into a control system. The proposed method addresses the challenge of creating time-optimal paths for drones, which is particularly difficult due to the need to account for non-linear dynamics and constraints. To overcome this, a new optimization problem is formulated, which incorporates the drone's non-linear characteristics and uses a specific type of control to ensure the drone follows the desired path. The resulting optimization problem is then solved using a combination of techniques, including a specific type of control and a method for approximating the drone's dynamics. The proposed method is demonstrated to be effective through simulations, which show that it can generate smooth, time-optimal trajectories for drones, even in the presence of complex constraints.

This study explores the internal composition of q-linear conjugate cyclic codes within the finite field of q powers, denoted as F_q. The internal structure of these codes is analyzed in terms of generator polynomials and specific matrix representations. Moreover, we establish a connection between the dual codes and their respective generator polynomials.

The  Community Forecasts Project (Community Forecasts Project, or CF2) of the High Energy Physics community has identified 11 critical issues for the future of HEP, which are crucial to address in the next decade. These concerns, which encompass infrastructure, collaboration, and career development, were discussed at a thematic meeting in Community Engagement Frontier Snowmass 2021. The resulting report outlines the community's recommendations, which are intended to serve as a guide for HEP and HEP investment stakeholders in achieving these goals.

This research presents a detailed analysis of the polarization of W bosons in tbar-t events, where a lepton and jets are detected, based on data collected by the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider. The data, recorded at a center-of-mass energy of 8 TeV and corresponding to a total integrated luminosity of 1.02 fb^-1, is used to investigate the polarization of W bosons in the tbar-t lepton+jets decay channel. The analysis involves the calculation of the angular distribution of leptons in the W boson rest frame, where the angle between the lepton and the W boson boost direction is determined. The findings are compared to predictions from the standard model, which indicate a polarization fraction of 0.68 for longitudinal W bosons, 0.29 for left-handed W bosons, and 0.11 for right-handed W bosons.

The first eigenvalue of the power hypernetwork, denoted $\lambda_{max}(H)$, is crucial in determining its spectral properties. A key inequality is established for $\lambda_{max}(H)$ in terms of the maximum degrees of the underlying graph $G$. Additionally, we identify the conditions under which a graph $G$ corresponds to a power hypernetwork, such that a given $\lambda_{max}(G)$ is its largest eigenvalue.

The massive scale of the Starlink constellation, comprising thousands of satellites, presents an opportunity to leverage it for various purposes, including precise location tracking. This research investigates the potential of the Starlink constellation for cooperative localization, focusing on the performance of the localization system and its limitations. The study derives mathematical bounds that determine the accuracy of the localization system, taking into account the positions of the satellites and the measurement errors. The research also explores the impact of the measurement errors on the localization system, and demonstrates that the accuracy of the localization system can be improved by using the satellites in a coordinated manner. The study provides numerical examples that illustrate the performance of the localization system, and shows that the accuracy of the localization system can be significantly improved by using the satellites in a coordinated manner.

The presence of transit timing variations in XO-3b's orbit suggests that its eccentricity is decreasing due to tidal forces, which is a result of its host star's rotation rate being slower than its orbital period. The observed changes in eccentricity and orbital period are consistent with theoretical models of tidal interactions, indicating that XO-3b's orbit will eventually become circular and synchronized with its host star's rotation within a few million years.

A crucial step in the analysis of 21-cm experiments is accurately determining the calibration parameters, which can be done using signal waves transmitted at regular intervals throughout the observation period. This paper presents a novel method for calibrating experiments like HERA and EDGES by combining the 21-cm data with multiple signal wave recordings, employing a Bayesian framework to jointly estimate calibration parameters and 21-cm brightness temperature. This approach is demonstrated to be effective using simulated HERA data, which shows that it can achieve precise calibration with a relative error of approximately 10% for all 100 calibration parameters, even in the presence of significant radio frequency interference. Furthermore, this method is shown to be capable of simultaneously calibrating the entire dataset, thereby providing a more comprehensive understanding of the 21-cm signal.

This research focuses on the application of the Atiyah-Bott fixed-point theorem to the computation of genus-zero, noncompactified, ordinary Gromov-Witten invariants for projective collections. The findings are used to establish the symmetrizability of the quantum product within the Grothendieck-Knudsen moduli space, and the process of symmetrization is explicitly described through a system of recursive equations. The general principle of symmetrization is also applicable to a broader category of Gromov-Witten invariants, and the computation results in a specific, previously unknown, intersection of three Hirzebruch divisors within the Grassmannian G(2,5).
This research examines the convergence of prime number theorems, specifically focusing on the $\mathcal{H}$-convergence, as well as the $\mathcal{K}$-convergence of the prime number theorem.

Alzheimer's disease trials often utilize longitudinal data to track the progression of the disease over time.  A common approach to analyzing this data is a mixed model, but it has limitations in its ability to model the shape of the treatment effect.  A new method has been developed that uses natural cubic splines to model the shape of the treatment effect, allowing for more accurate estimates of the treatment effect.  This method was applied to data from the A4A4A2A study, which investigated the effects of memantine on the progression of Alzheimer's disease.  The results showed that the new method was able to detect a significant treatment effect, whereas the traditional mixed model approach did not.  The new method has been found to be more accurate and efficient than the traditional approach, and it has been recommended for use in Alzheimer's disease trials.

This paper presents CRAWLING, a decentralized algorithm for smart parking systems that leverages crowdsourcing to enable vehicles to share parking information efficiently. CRAWLING enables parking sensors to communicate with each other, creating a network that facilitates the exchange of parking status updates. By utilizing this algorithm, vehicles can obtain up-to-date parking data, reducing the need for direct communication with parking sensors and minimizing the impact of sensor failures. The results of simulations demonstrate the effectiveness of CRAWLING in reducing the number of messages exchanged and the time required to detect parking sensor failures.

Recent studies have shown that training models with a restricted search space within each layer can achieve superior performance compared to traditional optimization methods. This paper delves into the geometric properties of the loss landscape in a single layer, specifically examining the local curvature at various points. Our analysis reveals that the local curvature at level-set minima is notably flatter compared to local minima, and this characteristic is more pronounced in networks with deeper layers. Our findings also indicate that as the depth of a network increases, the likelihood of encountering level-set minima that exhibit a flatter curvature also rises.

The effectiveness of word embeddings in NLP tasks is highly dependent on the context used to generate them. This study investigates the impact of different types of word contexts on various NLP tasks, including word analogy, word anagram, and word restoration. The analysis reveals that certain types of word contexts yield better results, and we also explore the relationship between context and word frequency.

We investigate the vertex partitioning problem for a specific type of random graph called the k-group model. In this model, we have $k$ groups of vertices, each with connections determined by their group assignment. Specifically, vertices within the same group have connections with probability $p_{in}$, while vertices from different groups have connections with probability $p_{out}$. We consider the case where $p_{in}$ is significantly larger than $p_{out}$, and we establish a threshold for the number of edges required to guarantee that a given graph realization can be colored with $k$ colors such that each color class forms a connected subgraph.

A novel approach to modeling rotating stars is presented, grounded in a Lagrangian framework. This formulation enables the representation of a rotating star as a fluid body with a non-uniformly rotating core, encapsulated within a singular, adaptable equation. The model is accompanied by a comprehensive set of equations that describe the system's behavior, including a key equation that governs the system's dynamics. The formulation is further refined by introducing a series of auxiliary equations that facilitate the solution of the system. The model is then applied to a variety of scenarios, including a study of the system's response to external forces, as well as a simulation of a rotating star's evolution over time. The results of the simulation reveal a striking degree of agreement between the model's predictions and those of a more traditional Eulerian approach, demonstrating the efficacy of the Lagrangian formulation in capturing the complex dynamics of rotating stars.

This study explores the properties of a generalized Lemaître-Tolman-Bondi (LTB) model within Palatini f(R) gravity, a modified theory of gravity. The model's behavior is analyzed using a specific f(R) function, which incorporates a cosmological constant, and its impact on the model's evolution is investigated. The results show that the model's behavior is significantly influenced by the choice of f(R) function, and that a specific function, which incorporates a cosmological constant, can lead to a model that is consistent with observations of the Hubble parameter and the luminosity distance of Type Ia supernovae. The model's behavior is also constrained by the luminosity distance of Type Ia supernovae, and its behavior is found to be consistent with observations of the Hubble parameter and the luminosity distance of Type Ia supernovae. The model's behavior is also constrained by the luminosity distance of Type Ia supernovae, and its behavior is found to be consistent with observations of the Hubble parameter and the luminosity distance of Type Ia supernovae.

A recent study has introduced a measure of nonlocality that is resistant to noise in quantum systems with multiple parts. This measure is based on the concept of robust nonlocality, which assesses the noise tolerance of quantum correlations. It has been demonstrated that this measure is a valid, system-independent metric for correlations in quantum systems with multiple parts. Furthermore, this measure is shown to be a subset of the original nonlocality measure, and it has been proven that the original nonlocality measure is maximized when the system is in a maximally entangled state. This measure is also shown to be a monotonically increasing quantity under local operations and classical communication.

This study introduces a method for predicting a user's visual focus within a computer interface, specifically a 160-millisecond window, using previously collected eye-tracking data. The proposed approach is based on a recurrent neural network with long-term memory capabilities, which is trained on the user's gaze data. The network's output is a probability distribution over the screen's pixels, representing the user's visual focus. The proposed method is validated using data from a study where participants viewed 120 seconds of a video, and the results demonstrate its ability to accurately predict the user's gaze at a specific time, with a correlation coefficient of 0.67. The proposed approach is also shown to outperform a baseline method, which simply predicts the user's gaze based on the previous time step, with a significant improvement in accuracy. The proposed method has potential applications in the field of human-computer interaction, where it can be used to improve the user experience by providing more accurate predictions of the user's visual focus.

A reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS) is a promising technology for future wireless networks, which can be used to enhance signal strength and coverage. This paper focuses on a specific type of RIS that can transmit signals, which is expected to be more effective in 6G wireless communications. We have developed a prototype of this transmissive RIS, which consists of 64 elements and can be controlled using 64-bit digital signals. We have also developed an algorithm that can be used to optimize the RIS's performance in a wireless network, and we have tested it using a real-world setup. Our results show that the transmissive RIS can significantly improve signal strength and coverage, and it can be a valuable addition to 6G wireless networks.

Offline reinforcement learning aims to find the best possible policy from a given dataset, without the option to gather new data.  A promising approach to this challenge is linear optimization, which can be used to find the best possible policy by solving a mathematical optimization problem.  In this paper, we revisit the linear optimization framework and show that it can be used to find the best possible policy with a wide variety of function approximations, including those that are not necessarily linear.  Our results demonstrate that the linear optimization framework can be used to find the best possible policy with a wide range of function approximations, including those that are not necessarily linear.  In addition, we show that the linear optimization framework can be used to find the best possible policy with a wide range of function approximations, including those that are not necessarily linear.  Our results have important implications for the development of efficient and scalable reinforcement learning algorithms.

This paper explores the concept of "homotopies for gratis!" which allows us to consider a category as a model for homotopy theory without additional structures. A category is useful as a homotopy theory for a certain type of "homotopy theory for gratis!" if it can be used to define all homotopy theories for that type. We introduce the notion of "tangent categories" which provide a foundational structure for a homotopy theory for gratis!. We then show that tangent categories can be obtained from tangent fibrations and demonstrate that tangent categories are equivalent to certain tangent fibrations. We also provide examples of tangent categories and their applications.

Our research indicates that the supermassive black hole in the galaxy J0437+2456 is surrounded by a turbulent, spherical accretion disk. This finding is based on the analysis of the galaxy's spectral energy distribution, which reveals a significant discrepancy between the observed and predicted infrared radiation. This discrepancy can be explained by the presence of a turbulent accretion disk with a mass accretion rate of approximately 0.0001 times the mass of the sun per second. This accretion rate is consistent with the galaxy's bolometric luminosity and suggests that the accretion disk is responsible for the observed infrared radiation. Furthermore, the presence of this accretion disk may be responsible for the galaxy's high star formation rate, which is significantly higher than expected for a galaxy of its mass.

This study explores the dynamics of a three-body system with varying masses, focusing on the stability of its linear arrangements. Specifically, we examine scenarios where two bodies intersect and collide, and where a body's position is defined by a complex coordinate in a three-dimensional space. By applying a mathematical model that accounts for collisions and varying masses, we derive an energy function and analyze its behavior in a mathematical space. Our results demonstrate that a specific configuration, where two bodies collide, is unstable and leads to a breakdown of the three-body system. Furthermore, we establish the existence of a specific type of unstable orbit, known as a homoclinic orbit, and demonstrate its connection to the system's collision dynamics.

A novel algorithm has been developed to deconvolve fluorescence lifetime imaging microscopy (FLIM) data, utilizing an iterative approach that incorporates total variation regularization and alternating direction method of multipliers. The algorithm's performance was assessed through simulations and experiments, demonstrating significant enhancements in both deconvolution and recovery of complex fluorescence lifetime distributions.

This study introduces a novel approach to product recommendation systems, which utilizes a graph-based model to predict user preferences. The proposed system leverages the strengths of graph convolutional networks to analyze user behavior, thereby enhancing its ability to provide accurate recommendations. The model's performance is evaluated using a real-world dataset, with results demonstrating its ability to effectively capture user preferences and provide relevant recommendations.

Deep manifold learning has proven effective in handling unlabelled data by uncovering hidden patterns. However, existing methods often rely on a separate clustering step to assign labels, which can be time-consuming and prone to errors. In contrast, this research presents an innovative unsupervised manifold labeled graph embedding technique that seamlessly integrates clustering and representation learning. By leveraging a novel loss function, the model can simultaneously learn an optimal graph representation and cluster data points, eliminating the need for separate steps. Experimental results on diverse datasets demonstrate the model's superior performance compared to state-of-the-art unsupervised methods.

In the context of grant-free access, a novel approach to designing sequences for high connectivity is proposed. The sequences are required to minimize inter-user interference, which is achieved by optimizing a specific objective function. A two-stage genetic algorithm is employed to find the optimal sequences, with the first stage focusing on optimizing the phase and the second on optimizing the amplitude. The performance of the proposed method is evaluated using the bit error rate, and its efficacy is demonstrated through simulations.

This research introduces a new, fully blind combinatorial coded sensing (CCS) technique, which is capable of identifying multiple targets without requiring knowledge of the coding scheme. CCS is an advanced method that enables simultaneous detection of multiple targets using a single sensor. Our proposed method involves developing a new algorithm called the potential function (PF) algorithm, which is used to determine the optimal target locations. This method is based on a mathematical model that represents the relationship between the target locations and the sensor readings. Our results show that the PF algorithm is effective in detecting multiple targets and its performance is superior to other existing methods. Our experiments also demonstrate that the PF algorithm is robust to noise and can accurately detect the target locations even in the presence of significant noise. Our results also show that the PF algorithm is computationally efficient and can be implemented in real-time. Our proposed CCS technique has the potential to be used in a wide range of applications, including surveillance, robotics, and environmental monitoring.

Deep learning models often struggle with generalization, particularly when faced with domain shifts. To address this issue, we've developed a novel approach that leverages adversarial and stochastic transformations to enhance model robustness. By applying these transformations to the source domain, we've found that the model's ability to adapt to the target domain is significantly improved. This approach, which we've dubbed Adversarial and Stochastic Transformations (AST), has been shown to outperform existing domain adaptation methods on a variety of datasets, including CIFAR10, CIFAR100, STL10, and ImageNet. Moreover, the model's ability to recover from the transformations has been found to be a key factor in its improved performance. To further enhance the model's robustness, we've also incorporated a novel technique called adversarial training, which has been shown to be effective in improving the model's ability to adapt to the target domain. Overall, our results demonstrate that the AST approach is a promising solution for improving the model's ability to generalize across different domains.

This research provides a characterization of 2-local and local derivations on Jordan matrix algebras, specifically over commutative rings equipped with an involution. The characterization is achieved by examining the associated derivations.

A well-established mathematical concept, the Dirac singularity, serves as a key example in various fields such as algebraic geometry, complex analysis, and potential applications in noncommutative geometry. This study delves into the mathematical properties of the Dirac singularity in the context of Berry's phase, specifically examining its impact on the electromagnetic field. By analyzing a specific scenario involving an electron traversing a closed path in the presence of the singularity, we derive the electromagnetic field and demonstrate that it is characterized by a magnetic field with a non-zero divergence and an electric field with a non-zero curl. This phenomenon is shown to be analogous to the Aharonov-Bohm effect, but with distinct features arising from the presence of the Dirac singularity.

This study explores the existence of compacton solutions in the context of a one-dimensional Bose-Einstein condensate with spin-orbit coupling. A novel form of the Gross-Pitaevskii equation is developed, which takes into account the density-dependent spin-orbit interaction. Our analysis reveals that the compacton's width is dependent on the strength of the spin-orbit coupling, and this dependence can be manipulated by adjusting the coupling strength. Consequently, our results provide a means to control the width of compacton in a Bose-Einstein condensate by leveraging the spin-orbit density reliance.

The discovery of the $\Lambda_c(2625)^+$ state by the LHCb collaboration has raised questions about its spin-parity and relationship to the $\Lambda_c(2595)^+$ state. This study investigates the spin-parity of the $\Lambda_c(2625)^+$ state and its possible connection to the $\Lambda_c(2595)^+$ state. It is found that the $\Lambda_c(2625)^+$ state is most likely the spin-parity counterpart of the $\Lambda_c(2595)^+$ state, specifically the $J^P = \frac{1}{2}^-$ state. This conclusion is supported by the heavy quark spin symmetry and the results of the $D$-wave $D^* \bar{K}$ molecular state analysis. It is also found that the $\Lambda_c(2625)^+$ state is a possible $D^* \bar{K}$ molecular state, and its mass and width are in good agreement with the experimental measurements. This study provides new insights into the structure of the $\Lambda_c(2625)^+$ state and its relationship to the $\Lambda_c(2595)^+$ state.

This research focuses on constructing sequences of piecewise constant functions from orbit spaces to Euclidean space that converge in the Lp-norm to a given continuous function. The necessary conditions for the existence of such sequences are also examined.

A comprehensive class of hypothetical particles known as Axion-Like Particles (ALPs) has been proposed to address theoretical and phenomenological issues in the Standard Model. These particles, which can be described by a relatively straightforward effective Lagrangian, have the potential to be discovered at high energy colliders. This white paper provides an in-depth analysis of the current experimental limits on ALPs at high energy muon colliders, identifies the key parameters that need to be studied, and outlines the future prospects for these particles at high energy muon colliders.

MetaSys is an open-source, cross-platform metadata administration tool that enables
the efficient management of metadata for software systems. MetaSys streamlines the
process of implementing and evaluating optimization techniques that span multiple
software design levels. The system is built using a modular architecture, allowing
for the seamless integration of multiple software design levels, including data,
object, and control. MetaSys is written in Java and is available for download on
GitHub.

In various applications, such as medical imaging, the availability of labeled data is often insufficient, making it challenging to develop effective machine learning models. To address this issue, researchers have explored the use of synthetic data and transfer learning techniques. This study investigates the effectiveness of combining these approaches, specifically by comparing the performance of synthetic data models and fine-tuned models based on pre-trained networks in a semi-supervised setting. The results show that synthetic data models outperform pre-trained networks, and a Siamese network-based fine-tuning method further improves performance, achieving a 10% increase in accuracy over the semi-supervised model.

This paper examines the long-term behavior of positive solutions to a specific set of nonlinear elliptic systems defined by the equations: $-\Delta u_i + V_i(x)u_i = \sum_{j=1}^N a_{ij} \phi_{\alpha_j}^j (x)$ for $i=1,\cdots,N$, where $u_i$ and $V_i(x)$ are non-negative functions, $\phi_{\alpha_j}^j (x)$ is a nonlinearity, and certain conditions on the parameters and functions are met. The study yields a sharp Pohozaev-type inequality and reveals that under specific conditions, no positive solutions exist.

Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) have been widely used for modeling sequential data, but they often struggle with learning long-term dependencies due to the vanishing gradient problem. To address this issue, researchers have proposed various solutions, including memory-augmented RNNs and RNNs with memory cells. However, these solutions can be computationally expensive and may not always yield optimal results. In this paper, we introduce a novel RNN architecture called the Fourier Recurrent Unit (FRU), which incorporates a Fourier transform-based memory cell to capture long-term dependencies. The FRU is designed to be lightweight and efficient, and it can be seamlessly integrated into existing RNN architectures. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the FRU through experiments on a range of tasks, including language modeling, sentiment analysis, and machine translation. The results show that the FRU outperforms traditional RNNs and other memory-augmented RNNs in terms of both accuracy and efficiency.

In Markov Decision Processes, we investigate the challenge of finding the most effective policy that maximizes rewards. We examine the efficiency of a specific algorithm, called the Navigating Algorithm, in identifying the optimal policy. This algorithm relies on a key metric, the distance to optimality, which measures the expected difference in rewards between the current policy and the best possible policy. We demonstrate that the Navigating Algorithm can find the optimal policy when the distance to optimality is a linear function of the state, and that it does so within a finite number of iterations. We also show that the algorithm is efficient when the distance to optimality is bounded, and that it can find the optimal policy within a finite number of iterations. Additionally, we provide a method for estimating the distance to optimality using a single sample from the states of the system. This allows us to determine the number of iterations required to find the optimal policy, and to evaluate the efficiency of the Navigating Algorithm in doing so.

A highly advanced method for generating extremely bright, ultrafast electron bunches with precise polarization has been proposed, which utilizes a dual-injection technique in an accelerating cavity. The approach involves injecting a preliminary electron wave packet into the cavity at a specific time, followed by injecting a secondary, higher-energy electron wave packet at a later time. The interaction of these electrons with the cavity's electromagnetic fields results in the creation of electron bunches with precise polarization and sub-cycle temporal structure. The method is versatile and can be used to generate electron bunches with linear, circular, or elliptical polarization, as well as to produce bunches with precise temporal characteristics. The approach is based on the interaction of the electrons with the cavity's electromagnetic fields, which can be controlled by adjusting the injection timing and energy of the electrons. The method is also applicable to the generation of electron bunches with precise energy and momentum distributions. The approach is versatile and can be used to generate electron bunches with precise polarization and temporal characteristics.

The origins of life and its evolution on Earth are closely linked to the development of the universe's increasing complexity. This research explores the connection between the growth of complexity in the universe and the emergence of life, as well as the role of life in the universe's complexity growth. This investigation also examines the potential for life to arise in other parts of the universe, as well as the implications of the universe's increasing complexity for the emergence of life and the development of intelligent life.

The exponential growth of scientific literature poses a significant challenge for policy makers in identifying relevant research. To address this issue, we developed a novel approach that leverages open repositories and artificial intelligence to facilitate policy makers in navigating the vast landscape of scientific literature. Our approach is demonstrated through a comprehensive analysis of 1,200 publications on climate change, utilizing a machine learning model to identify key research topics and trends. The results of our study reveal a significant correlation between research funding and publication output, highlighting the need for a more equitable distribution of research funding. Furthermore, we discuss the potential applications of our approach in supporting policy makers in making informed decisions about research and development priorities.

The mobile market is dominated by Android, and its underlying components are crucial to its success. However, the mobile platform's widespread adoption has led to increased security concerns. The mobile operating system's core components, including the Android Native Development Kit (NDK), are particularly vulnerable to security threats. The NDK's side-channel vulnerabilities have been understudied, and this research aims to address this gap by developing a tool called a Side-channel Vulnerability Analysis and Assessment tool (ASVAAN). This tool is designed to identify potential vulnerabilities in the NDK, and its effectiveness is demonstrated through its application to a popular open-source library. The results of this research highlight the importance of side-channel analysis in the NDK and provide a foundation for future research in this area.

The Ethereum blockchain's open-source nature has enabled the creation of innovative applications, but it has also been exploited for malicious purposes. As a result, there is a pressing need to study the Ethereum network's behavior and identify potential threats. To address this, we introduce a novel approach to analyze the Ethereum network as a series of transaction graphs, each representing a specific time frame. By examining these graphs, we can identify and track the evolution of subgraphs, which can be used to detect anomalies and potential threats. Our research involves a detailed analysis of the Ethereum network's transaction patterns, including the identification of subgraphs with specific labels, such as those associated with high-risk activities. Our findings reveal that the Ethereum network's transaction patterns exhibit certain characteristics, such as a high degree of clustering and a power-law distribution of node degrees. We also observe that the network's transaction patterns exhibit significant temporal variations, which can be used to identify potential anomalies. Our research contributes to the growing body of knowledge on the Ethereum network and provides a foundation for future research in this area.

The LaAlO$_3$/SrTiO$_3$ interface is a well-known site for the emergence of a two-dimensional electron system, which has been extensively researched. However, the interface's underlying mechanism and its associated properties remain unclear. In this study, we utilized terahertz spectroscopy to investigate the interface's optical properties and discovered a series of resonances in the terahertz frequency range. These resonances were identified as optical phonon modes of the SrTiO$_3$ substrate, which were influenced by the interface's unique characteristics. Furthermore, we observed that the interface's electron system exhibited a significant screening effect, which was found to be dependent on the interface's carrier density. These findings provide new insights into the interface's properties and its potential applications in the development of novel electronic devices.

We examine the complexity of two related proof systems: one based on BV and another on pomset logic. In the first system, we demonstrate that proving a theorem in BV is a problem of NP-completeness, and we develop a polynomial-time algorithm to transform any proof into a normal form. Coastal flooding is a pressing issue that affects a significant portion of the global population, with the situation expected to worsen due to climate change. To address this challenge, a digital twin of Earth's coasts has been proposed, which would enable the creation of a real-time, physics-informed model for predicting coastal flooding. This model would be based on a rapid and efficient numerical approach, leveraging a combination of advanced machine learning techniques and a cutting-edge numerical method. The Turing instability is a phenomenon where a system's pattern formation is triggered by the interaction between diffusion and reaction processes. In this study, we explore the effects of finite transmission rates on the Turing patterns that emerge in reaction-diffusion systems connected through a network. We find that finite transmission rates can lead to the formation of new Turing patterns, which are distinct from those observed in idealized systems with infinite transmission rates. Our results are supported by numerical simulations and provide insight into the complex dynamics of pattern formation in reaction-diffusion systems.

The quantization of Yang-Mills theory reveals that the gauge field's quantum fluctuations are negligible, allowing for a quasi-classical interpretation. This implies that the gauge field's quantum behavior can be described within a framework that closely resembles its classical properties. Specifically, the quasi-classical approximation of the gauge field's wave function can be formulated as a complex-valued expression, where the real component represents a classical gauge field configuration.

The optical properties of nanowires are heavily influenced by their lateral confinement, resulting in the polarization of light being affected by the wire's orientation. Our research focuses on the behavior of light polarization in GaAs/AlGaAs w-GaN quantum wires, which exhibit strong spatial confinement. We have developed a theoretical model that accurately predicts the wire's optical response, taking into account the confinement and the material's properties. Our model reveals that the wire's emission spectrum consists of two main components, corresponding to the light's polarization along and perpendicular to the wire's axis. We have also investigated the effect of wire orientation on the polarization of light, which is found to be highly dependent on the wire's orientation. Our results show that the light polarization can be controlled by adjusting the wire's orientation, which has significant implications for the development of optoelectronic devices.

In the realm of negotiation dialogues, understanding the adversary's intentions is crucial for achieving a successful negotiation outcome. To this end, we've developed a new task that involves predicting adversary statements based on observed intentions, using a dataset created through data augmentation. Our proposed model, incorporating a transformer-based architecture, outperforms existing approaches in both intent and statement prediction tasks.

We investigate the behavior of light rays in a spacetime resulting from compactifying a higher-dimensional spacetime with dynamical string tension, particularly in the context of a model with $D=4+N$ dimensions. Our analysis reveals that the effective four-dimensional spacetime can be represented as a Friedmann-Robertson-Walker metric with a specific scale factor, and we find that the four-dimensional spacetime is conformally flat. We then examine the behavior of light rays in the vicinity of the compactified spacetime and determine the conditions under which they can escape to infinity. Our results suggest that the behavior of light rays in the vicinity of the compactified spacetime is similar to that of a black hole, and we discuss the implications of our findings for the study of braneworlds and string theory.

In the context of online experiments, researchers often employ sequential trials to gather more data, but the traditional A/B testing method can be inefficient when it comes to identifying treatment effects. To address this, a novel approach called Pigeonhole Design has been developed, drawing inspiration from the stable matching problem. This method aims to minimize the number of participants who receive inconsistent treatments, thereby enhancing the efficiency of sequential trials. By formulating the problem as a stable matching issue, researchers have developed a fast algorithm to implement Pigeonhole Design, which has been tested through simulations and real-world experiments. The results indicate that Pigeonhole Design outperforms traditional randomization methods in terms of statistical power, making it a more effective choice for sequential trials.

The interface between Si and Al2O3 plays a crucial role in determining the reliability of modern MOSFETs, and understanding its properties is essential for developing advanced devices. In this study, we investigated the properties of the Si/Al2O3 interface using a combination of first-principles calculations and experimental techniques. Our results show that the interface exhibits a positive charge of approximately 0.15e per unit cell, which is consistent with previous experimental findings. Our analysis also reveals that the presence of Si-O and O-Si-O bonds at the interface is responsible for the formation of the clear interface. Furthermore, we found that the energy levels associated with these bonds are responsible for the low density of interface states, which contributes to the high quality of the Si/Al2O3 interface. Our research provides new insights into the properties of the Si/Al2O3 interface and has important implications for the development of advanced devices.

The study of black holes is a fundamental aspect of general relativity, and the formation of black holes is a complex process that involves a critical collapse. This is achieved by using nonlinear statistical methods to analyze the data obtained from numerical simulations. Our results show that the critical collapse solutions in a toroidal geometry exhibit a universal behavior, characterized by a critical exponent of 1.32. This finding is consistent with previous studies, and it suggests that the critical collapse solutions in a toroidal geometry are similar to those in a spherical geometry. Our study also reveals that the critical collapse solutions in a toroidal geometry are sensitive to the initial conditions, and that the initial conditions can significantly affect the critical exponent. This finding is important for understanding the critical collapse process in various geometries, and it has implications for the study of black holes in general relativity.

The anomaly detection problem is a complex task that involves identifying unusual patterns in data. To address this issue, researchers have developed numerous methods, each with its own strengths and limitations. In this study, we investigate the effectiveness of a diverse set of anomaly detection techniques, including those based on statistical analysis, clustering, and deep learning. We evaluate these methods on a range of datasets and assess their performance using a common framework. Our results provide valuable insights into the relative merits of different approaches and highlight the importance of selecting the right technique for a given problem.

Brain tumors are a significant global health issue, with the number of cases rising rapidly. Accurate diagnosis and treatment planning for these tumors rely heavily on precise segmentation of tumors from MRI images. However, the complexity of brain tumors and the limitations of current segmentation methods have made this task challenging. This study presents a novel approach to brain tumor segmentation using convolutional neural networks and efficient post-processing techniques. By employing a combination of these methods, the proposed approach achieves accurate segmentation results while minimizing computational costs. The study's results demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, with the proposed segmentation method achieving a Dice coefficient of 0.85 and a Jaccard index of 0.79. The proposed approach is particularly well-suited for use in clinical settings, where it can provide accurate segmentation results within a reasonable timeframe.

This study addresses the challenge of reconstructing a broad-band acoustic wave speed distribution from scattered pressure data. A novel, lossless, and flexible neural network architecture is introduced, leveraging the physical characteristics of the inverse scattering problem to improve neural network performance. The network's design incorporates translation invariance, wave propagation symmetry, and scaling invariance, allowing for the efficient and accurate recovery of wave speed distributions. This study focuses on an optimal degradation testing strategy for systems with two interdependent components, where component lifetimes follow a bivariate gamma distribution and are linked through shared parameters. The research aims to minimize the expected total testing cost, subject to constraints on component lifetimes and a specified failure probability threshold, by developing an optimization model and solving it using a numerical approach. The effectiveness of the proposed model is demonstrated through a numerical example and its practical application is showcased in the context of a bearing reliability case study.

The study of triangular flow $v_3$ in Au+Au and Cu+Au collisions at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider's 200 GeV energy level is examined. Results from a multiphase transport model are compared with experimental data and theoretical predictions from initial spatial anisotropies. The model reveals that initial spatial anisotropies significantly impact $v_3$ at early collision stages, while the model's predictions align with experimental data for Cu+Au collisions but overestimate the Au+Au $v_3$ values.

The interaction between coronal mass ejections and high-speed streams is a crucial aspect of solar wind behavior, significantly influencing the space environment. This study focuses on the unique characteristics of a high-speed stream within a coronal mass ejection event, specifically the 2015 Halloween storm. By analyzing the plasma's polytropic index, we discovered a distinct value of 1.2 within the high-speed stream, contrasting with the surrounding sheath and reverse stream regions, where the index varied between 1.4 and 2.0. This finding suggests that the high-speed stream's unique index is a result of its plasma's behavior during the coronal mass ejection event, specifically the heating and expansion processes that occur within it.

This article presents a computational method for modeling the random waypoint mobility pattern in wireless ad hoc networks. In such networks, each node randomly selects a target location and travels there at a set speed, before pausing at the destination for a predetermined time period. Following this, the process repeats with the node either selecting a new destination or stopping movement if it reaches its maximum number of trips. A detailed explanation of the underlying mathematical principles and a corresponding algorithm are provided in this study.

The $K^+K^-$ invariant mass spectrum is studied in detail, particularly in the region around 2 GeV $m_{\rm eff}$, where the mass is calculated using the sum of the three-momenta of the constituent particles divided by $c$. The analysis is based on data from $pp$ collisions at 1.3 TeV, collected by the ALICE detector at the LHC, and is compared to predictions from PYTHIA 8.2 and HERWIG 7 Monte Carlo simulations. The observed excess in the $K^+K^-$ spectrum at $2\,m_K$ is found to be consistent with background expectations from $q\bar{q}$ annihilation and $J/\psi$ decays, and is not significant enough to be attributed to a new particle.

The microscopic collective motion of a many-body system is investigated using the time-dependent density matrix formalism, and the effect of single-particle motion on the collective motion is taken into account. The study of a spherical nucleus's breathing mode is conducted, and the impact of nucleonic effective mass on the inertia is examined. The calculated inertia values are found to be significantly influenced by the effective mass, and the results are compared to those obtained from the cranking approximation. The study also explores the effect of collective pair correlations on the inertia values. The findings are relevant to understanding the properties of nuclear reactions, such as the giant monopole mode and the giant dipole mode.

The Representation and Reasoning Corpus (RRCorpus) is a collection of logical reasoning problems sourced from the web, annotated with formal proofs. To tackle RRCorpus problems, we propose an innovative approach that involves a two-part process: initially, we utilize graph-based representations to model the problem, and then employ search algorithms to identify proofs. Our method encompasses two distinct graph formats, one for propositional problems and another for more complex first-order problems. By utilizing these graph models, we can effectively represent and reason about RRCorpus problems, leveraging their inherent structure to facilitate efficient search. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, yielding promising results in solving a range of RRCorpus problems.

The flux function's lack of continuity at a specific point x_c leads to unique solution characteristics. We demonstrate that the solution is stable with respect to the initial condition in a specific function space, where the stability exponent is influenced by the smoothness of the flux function at x_c. The stability exponent is also dependent on the flux function's growth rate at infinity. Our proof relies on a specific method that combines the properties of the flux function's growth rate and its continuity at x_c.

This research explores the spectral efficiency of cell-free massive MIMO systems utilizing MC-DD, where a large number of access points communicate with a user through orthogonal frequency subcarriers. The channel conditions are assumed to be known at the APs, and the users are unaware of their own channel state. The uplink and downlink MC-DD spectral efficiency is analyzed under two scenarios: one where the subcarrier allocation is optimized and the other where it is not. The results show that, under optimal allocation, cell-free massive MIMO with MC-DD achieves a spectral efficiency that is proportional to the number of APs, whereas under non-optimal allocation, the spectral efficiency is constant regardless of the number of APs. The research also provides insights into the effects of subcarrier allocation and the impact of inter-carrier interference on the spectral efficiency.

We introduce a method for accurately measuring the impact of a specific dataset on a machine learning model trained using differentially private stochastic gradient descent, with a particular focus on shuffle differentially private models. Our approach involves a single pass through the data, and it's possible to determine the effect of an individual's data on the final model with a single update step. Our findings show that the impact of an individual's data on the model is equivalent to the model's sensitivity to that individual's data in the original non-private setting. Our method is applicable to a broad range of models, including those that use a Gaussian mechanism for privacy protection, and it's particularly effective in scenarios where the data is large and the number of users is relatively small.

This paper introduces a novel modulation technique called Orthogonal Time Frequency Multiplexing (OTFM) that offers a new approach to wireless communication. The proposed OTFM modulation combines the key benefits of two existing methods, Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiplexing (OFDM) and Cyclic Prefix (CP) OFDM. The OTFM modulation achieves the same low complexity receiver as CP-OFDM while providing the same spectral efficiency as OFDM. The paper presents the analysis of OTFM and its application in MIMO systems, and it also develops a low-complexity receiver for MIMO-OTFM channels. The results show that the proposed OTFM outperforms CP-OFDM in terms of performance and its receiver is more efficient than the one for MIMO-OFDM channels.

This article explores the operator norm on $\ell^1(S, \mu)$, a weighted algebra associated with a discrete semigroup $S$ and a weight function $\mu$. We establish that the operator norm of a convolution operator $T_\lambda$ in $\ell^1(S, \mu)$ can be expressed as the supremum of the absolute values of $\lambda(s) \mu(s)$ for elements in $S$. Additionally, we demonstrate that $T_\lambda$ is invertible if and only if the reciprocals of the absolute values of $\lambda(s) \mu(s)$ for elements in $S$ are uniformly bounded.

The proliferation of intelligent public transport vehicles is driven by the need for real-time data processing and analysis, which can be achieved through mobile edge computing. However, these vehicles often face the challenge of limited connectivity due to their movement and the resulting low signal strength. To address this issue, a novel system is proposed that integrates wireless power transfer and energy harvesting from a mobile edge computing server. A smart reflecting surface is employed to enhance the system's performance by optimizing the server's beamforming and surface reflection coefficients, as well as the server's location. A joint optimization approach is used to maximize the server's energy harvesting and computing capabilities, taking into account the energy constraints and the resulting optimization problem. A suboptimal solution is developed using the successive convex approximation method, which involves a two-stage optimization process. Simulation results demonstrate the system's effectiveness in terms of energy harvesting and computing performance.

We investigate the degree of a formula, which is the highest number of variables within any of its terms. We introduce a method to estimate a formula's degree when it is given in a specific format, such as DNF or CNF. Our approach yields a more precise result for formulas in DNF format, surpassing a previous upper bound established by Alon, Krivelevich, and Szemer\'edi. We also establish a method to estimate the degree of formulas in CNF format, which, to the best of our knowledge, represents the first result in this area.

This research examines a specific class of systems described by the equation $\dot{x} = f(x) - x$, where $f$ is a smooth function with a bounded range. A key focus is on the existence of at least two equilibrium points, which leads to the existence of non-trivial invariant sets. To address this, a novel approach is developed, utilizing a modified version of the Conley index to detect the presence of equilibrium pairs. This method is then applied to biological systems, specifically the FitzHugh-Nagumo model, to demonstrate its effectiveness in detecting bistable states.

This study examines the structure of a strange quark star with spin polarization and a magnetic field at a finite temperature. We use the MIT bag model to describe quarks and incorporate a magnetic field into our model. We derive a Lagrangian that includes Nambu-Jona-Lasinio interactions and calculate quark properties using the Dirac equation. We then determine the equation of state and calculate the mass-radius relationship for spin polarized strange quark stars in the presence of a magnetic field at a finite temperature. Our results show that spin polarization and magnetic fields have a significant impact on the star's structure, with higher magnetic fields and temperatures leading to smaller star radii and masses. We also find that spin polarization increases the maximum mass of the star, while higher temperatures have the opposite effect.

Deep learning models have achieved remarkable success in various audio-visual tasks, including speech recognition, speaker identification, and music analysis. This success can be attributed to the ability of these models to capture intricate correlations between audio and visual information. This survey delves into the recent advancements in deep audio-visual correlation learning, focusing on the development of novel architectures, the extraction of meaningful features, and the integration of prior knowledge. Furthermore, the survey highlights the potential of this field and identifies key challenges that need to be addressed to achieve further breakthroughs.

This study explores the probability of optimal solutions in the Linear Ordering Problem, a complex problem that involves maximizing a quadratic function with specific constraints. By introducing a probabilistic model, we investigate the properties of optimal solutions and their relationship to the problem's input data. Our analysis reveals that the problem of determining the probability of an optimal solution is NP-hard, and we develop a method to calculate this probability efficiently. Furthermore, we propose a new algorithm that leverages this insight to find an optimal solution with high probability.

Theoretical models of superconducting transitions have been extensively studied, but experimental data on granular superconducting films have been challenging to explain. In this study, we investigate the behavior of NbN films with varying thicknesses and focus on the resistance characteristics of the films in the granular regime. We find that the films exhibit a critical temperature of around 10 K, but their resistance behavior is more complex than predicted by existing models. In particular, we observe a significant increase in the slope of the resistance curve as the temperature approaches the critical temperature, and this increase is accompanied by a significant decrease in the resistance. We attribute these effects to the inhomogeneous distribution of superconducting and normal states in the films, and we propose a model that takes into account the effects of the films' granularity on their resistance characteristics.

The query result is the set of matches of r in the graph, with each match being a sequence of edges. The query result is then projected onto the time dimension, resulting in a set of time points. We show that temporal regular trail queries can be evaluated in polynomial time, with respect to the size of the input graph and the regular expression. The $Li_3$ radicals were generated through a 266 nm laser interacting with $Li$ atoms and $CH_3I$ molecules. The effectiveness of the slower was confirmed by observing the reduction in the laser-induced fluorescence signal when the cooling laser power was increased. The findings suggest that the Swift X-ray transient identifier is capable of detecting transients in real-time, making it a valuable tool for the study of X-ray transients.

A bilateral trade flow is a flow between two parties, where one is a buyer and the other is a seller. In order to analyze the data, a three-dimensional panel data model is used to break down bilateral trade flows into distinct components. The model accounts for the interdependence between the two parties, allowing for the separation of the flows into distinct elements. The elements include the average level of trade, the unique characteristics of the buyer and seller, and the interaction between the two parties. The interaction between the buyer and seller is further divided into the exchange of goods and the net transfer of goods. The model is applied to international trade data, and the results show that the model is able to accurately capture the dynamics of bilateral trade. The model is also used to estimate the impact of various factors on bilateral trade, such as the exchange rate and the terms of trade. The results show that the model is able to provide useful insights into the dynamics of bilateral trade.

This research introduces a novel approach to equalizing linear quantum systems with Gaussian dynamics, utilizing consistent, analytically derived feedback control. Unlike traditional methods, our technique does not necessitate the use of infinite energy or a Hamiltonian interaction between the system and controller. The proposed feedback control method is capable of equalizing any linear quantum system, resulting in a controlled system with a flat spectral density across all frequencies. The efficacy of this method is demonstrated through the successful equalization of a single-mode bosonic field, subject to both dissipation and nonlinearity.

Time perception duration (TPD) has been found to be a significant indicator of mental health, and research has shown that it can be used to identify and monitor conditions such as depression, anxiety, and schizophrenia. Studies have established that TPD is linked to changes in brain activity, particularly in the prefrontal cortex, and that it can be used to detect and track the progression of these conditions. However, current methods for assessing TPD are often limited to controlled settings and fail to capture real-world variations in TPD. To address these limitations, we have developed a novel approach that uses machine learning to predict TPD in real-time, based on data from wearable devices. Our approach has been tested on a dataset of 100 participants and has shown promising results, with a mean absolute error of 10.4 minutes and a mean absolute percentage error of 10.3%. Our findings suggest that TPD can be used as a reliable and practical tool for monitoring mental health, and that it can be used to identify and track changes in TPD over time.

In a field experiment, we investigated how the balance between speed and accuracy in decision-making is influenced by the complexity of the task. The study took place in a high-stakes environment where doctors made life-or-death decisions about which patients to resuscitate. By manipulating the time available for decision-making, we found that doctors made faster but less accurate decisions when under time pressure, and vice versa. The results showed that when doctors were more accurate, they were more likely to make the optimal decision. The study also revealed that doctors' performance was significantly affected by their level of expertise, with more experienced doctors making more accurate decisions, especially when given more time. The findings suggest that in complex decision-making tasks, the quality of the decision is more important than the speed at which it is made.

The fairness of AI systems is a pressing concern, yet there is no universally accepted definition of fairness in AI systems, leading to a proliferation of fairness metrics and guidelines. This lack of clarity has resulted in inconsistent and often contradictory recommendations for fairness in AI systems. In an effort to address this issue, we examine the legal implications of fairness definitions and assess their consistency. Our analysis reveals that some fairness definitions are not legally sound, and we propose a framework for evaluating the legal consistency of fairness definitions. This framework is based on a comprehensive review of relevant laws and regulations, and we use it to evaluate a range of fairness definitions. Our results suggest that many existing definitions of fairness are not legally sound, and we provide a set of recommendations for developing more consistent and legally sound definitions of fairness in AI systems.

The weak interaction's parity violation effect is observed in atomic systems as a difference in energy levels between states of opposite parity. This phenomenon is investigated in the context of the atomic nucleus, where a theoretical model is proposed to explain how the weak interaction can cause a change in magnetization in the nucleus. The model is based on the idea that the weak interaction can cause a transition between nuclear states with different parity, resulting in a change in the nucleus' magnetic moment. The model is tested using a specific type of ion, a trivalent lanthanoid ion, and the results are compared to experimental data. The model's predictions are also used to explain a phenomenon known as the neutrino pair discharge effect, where the nucleus emits a pair of neutrinos. The model's predictions are found to be consistent with experimental data, and the results suggest that the weak interaction can cause a change in the magnetization of the nucleus.

The first observation of the $\Lambda$ hyperon in a helium-4 nucleus was made in 2014, and subsequently, researchers have discovered various other hypernuclei. In this study, we investigate single- and double-strangeness hypernuclei up to mass number 8, specifically the $\Lambda$, $(\Lambda,\Lambda')$, $\Sigma$, $(\Sigma,\Lambda)$, and $\Xi$ sectors. We employ the CHiral Effective Field Theory to calculate the CHPT hyperon electromagnetic form factors, which are then used to determine the CHPT hypernuclear magnetic moments. We also calculate the CHPT hypernuclear quadrupole moments. Our research demonstrates that the CHPT hypernuclear magnetic moments and quadrupole moments are in good agreement with experimental data.

The proliferation of social media platforms has led to a growing concern about user privacy. In response, the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) has been implemented to safeguard user data. However, the existing regulations are insufficient to address the complexities of social media, where users' data is often shared with third-party applications. To address this, the proposed paper introduces MetaPriv, a novel system that empowers users to manage their data privacy on social media platforms. By integrating a meta-layer, MetaPriv enables users to set granular privacy policies for third-party applications, ensuring that their data remains secure. The system's architecture is designed to be adaptable, allowing users to easily modify their privacy policies as needed. The effectiveness of MetaPriv is demonstrated through a case study, showcasing its ability to protect user data on real-world social media platforms.

We investigate the branching process in a changing environment, specifically its coalescent point process, which is derived from the point process of the branching process itself. The coalescent point process is found to be self-similar, and we establish a criterion for it to be a Malthusian coalescent, which is characterized by an exponentially distributed inter-birth times and exponential inter-generation times.

We examine a high-temperature spin model on a countable graph, characterized by a countable set of spin values, resulting in a uncountable set of distinct Gibbs measures, thereby expanding on a prior count-measure result for uncountable spin value sets.

We have compiled a comprehensive catalog of these galaxies, which includes 120,000 objects with a central speed dispersion of 10 km/s or more. The catalog is based on a selection criterion that ensures a high degree of reliability in the measured parameters. We have analyzed the properties of the selected galaxies, including their central speed dispersion, mass, and structural parameters, and found that they are consistent with previous studies. We have also investigated the relationship between the measured parameters and found that the measured central speed dispersion correlates with the mass of the galaxies, and that the measured parameters are consistent with the predictions of the stellar population synthesis models.
